title: My Life: Mildred Frances Lewis Turley
text:
My Early School Days and Activities
This chapter tells you about my elementary school experiences, from learning to read and do basic math, to my teachers, and all the fun we had during recess.
I remember struggling with reading because I would go too fast. Finally, a teacher told me if I didn’t read slowly enough to tell her what I’d read, she would tell Doris to tell my mother I wouldn’t be home for lunch. Oh boy, I read it slow enough! I didn’t want to miss lunch, so I slowed up and read it, and I told him what was in it. I really did learn how to add, multiply, subtract, and write. Then I went into 4th grade, and that teacher taught me. In 5th grade, my teacher was Mr. Hat, and I liked him. He didn’t teach the next year, so my Uncle Charlie Whipple was my teacher in 6th grade, and he was a good teacher too. When I got up into 9th grade, my teacher wasn’t very helpful, and I saw one boy being tormented by another student in the class.
School started every morning with a bell on the hill, ringing about half an hour before it was time to go to school. The principal or one of the teachers would ring it. They did the same thing for recess, at lunchtime, and then when it was time to go home at night. At recess, we used to play on the “Giants side”. I lost so many shoes riding down it, but I loved to ride down the slide and swings. We would also play baseball. In the wintertime, when it was snowy, we had sleds – they don’t have many anymore – but we would take them to school. During recess, we’d slide down the hill; we had more fun falling down that hill on the sled. While some children stayed at school for lunch, I always liked to go home unless it was a really cold and sunny day. I forgot to tell you that in the 2nd grade, I had a cousin, Uncle Archie’s daughter, and then Shirley and Obie’s Grant, whom we used to play with a lot. We would sometimes squabble and argue. I remember one day, my cousin Sybil fainted in school. I don’t know what caused the fainting, but when school was out, I went running home and told my Mama, “Guess what, I got a name here!”.
My High School Years and Personal Trials
This chapter covers my transition to high school, a significant injury that impacted my education, and my experiences with seminary classes.
After I made it through 8th grade, it was time for graduation, and I was just so excited to be graduating to high school. I knew I was going to have a different experience there. I remember our graduation exercises, the dress I wore, and the shoes. I was even allowed to give my office, which I thought was really something. I had a real nice summer, and then it was time to start high school. I can’t remember just how long I had been going to school as a freshman, not too long, I don’t think.
We had hand water in our house, and I was heating water on the stove for washing up and getting ready for school. The night before, someone had dropped the axe on the floor, and I didn’t know it was there. When I went across with the hand water, I stepped on it and split my foot. It was so painful. They didn’t have doctors like they do now. I remember my mom and daddy talking about taking me to the hospital, but they never did. So, my foot had been partially broken, and it had to heal on its own. I remember having to learn to walk all over again by pushing a chair. That was so painful; to this day, I don’t know how I survived it. I never even had any pain pills or anything. I had hoped to go on to be a sophomore next year, but the principal wouldn’t let me. He made me take my freshman year over again.
I took seminary when I was in high school. They had ‘release time’ classes to go to seminary. I did not like my seminary teacher. I took three years of seminary, and when it got time for us to graduate, he didn’t have a diploma for me! I just couldn’t believe that, since I had completed my work. But I kept pestering him until he found and got me my diploma. When we went to get our diplomas, I was the only one that didn’t get one initially.
My Post-High School Work and Community Contributions
This chapter details my diverse work experiences after high school, the impact of national events like Pearl Harbor, and my significant act of community giving.
I think it was probably the summer after maybe my sophomore or junior year; I don’t remember what year it was, but anyway, my cousin Ellen, who had been living in Taylor, got married in September 1939. We used to go down and visit with them quite a bit. She lived in her own little home. We really did like to go visit with her and stay with her. Then she moved out into the Monthly Ranch, and we would go out there and stay with her also. In 1941, my brother died in January, and my relatives Marbury and Carl were married on July 26th that same year.
Doris and I went down and got a summer job at the Air Force Base in Douglas, where her brother Lester was a fireman. So we went down and spent the summer with him. Doris was a teletype operator, and I worked in what they called the ‘wagon apartment’. I would go around selling hot coffee, donuts, popcorn, candy, gum, and other snacks. I remember when I’d go around, I’d say, “Hot coffee! Donuts! Popcorn, candy!” and they would come running. The Japanese bombed Pearl Harbor on December 7, 1941. After that, things had to be rationed; I remember sugar and gas, and quite a few other things. While I was on this summer job, I saved quite a bit of money. I really did enjoy that summer down there. We met many good people, including a boy from Mesa, Arizona, whom I thought was a pretty nice boy. I wanted so badly for him to ask me out.
I graduated from high school in 1947. After I graduated, I started working an all-night shift, but I didn’t like it because I had to sleep during the day. Then, Doris and I got a job as waitresses at the Paint Pony Lodge for Mary and Eric. They had a few rooms they rented out, mostly serving people who stayed there, but they also took people off the highway. We quite liked the job; we really made good money there. I remember one evening, four or five people came in. Doris told me, “You can take those people,” and she would take her own. So I took their order, and they ordered meals. I realized they must be Mormons and they said, “Yes, I’m Brother John Longdon, and we’re down from Salt Lake for a convention”. I got to wait on them, and they gave me good tips. I was really glad Doris let me wait on them because I got better tips that way. I would save my money, putting my tips in a jar on my bed every night, and put my check in the bank. I finally got $100 from that job.
I said to my parents, “What can I do? I wonder if I’d like to do something good”. I always paid my tithing. We were building a chapel on the hill for the old troops, and we really needed supplies. I said, “I know what I’m going to do! I’m going to take this $100 over and give it to Bishop Built for the donations to build the fund”. I went over and handed Bishop Built the money, and he emptied the dollars out. I said, “I want you to use it for the building”. There was $100 there, and he just didn’t believe I would do that, to donate $100 to the building. Doris, I think, got mad at me for that, and we quit our job out there.1
My next job was with Wayne Bartlett, and sometimes he wanted me to work on Sundays. I went through a dilemma, praying about whether I should work on Sunday. I finally just decided on my own that I knew my mom didn’t want me to work on Sunday, so I told him I wouldn’t. Then, my next job was with a German man at a service station.
The Call to Mission and Pre-Departure Events
Even though I wanted to get married, I received an exciting mission call, and my family and I made preparations for my journey.
While I still hadn’t married, and I wanted to get married so badly, I finally got my mission call! I was so excited that it was to Alberta, Canada. I knew it was going to be cold up there, and I told them they had to build me a different home. However, one source also states the mission call was to “American Fork, Utah”. As I got ready for my mission, my cousin, who is a genealogist, Paul Lilly, and Doris, helped me. We were in Salt Lake City, and my cousin was proposed to and became engaged to be married in January. I went down to get my mission. They got married in January.
My Journey and Arrival at Mission
My journey to the mission was quite eventful, involving a long, uncomfortable train ride and a derailment, before I finally arrived at the mission headquarters.
Dorothy and Herman, who were now engaged, stayed in Salt Lake with me until it was time for my flight into Canada. They didn’t fly with me. I got on the train with four other women, and one of these girls was going to the same mission as I was. As the train left Salt Lake, I could still see Doris and Herman waving and standing by, and the more we went, the more homesick I got. I had never left home before. We got up to Montana, and the train derailed, so we had to get off the train. I needed my passport for the Canadian border to get into Canada. We got on another train, but it only had one passenger car, and the rest was very bumpy. The Canadian food was unappetizing; I just couldn’t get hungry enough to eat that lunch. With all the bumping around, I kept saying we couldn’t ever eat that food.
At nighttime, they put up the berths for us to sleep in. They told us they would get the berths ready, and then they’d come back and let us know. We waited and waited, and finally, we walked up there ourselves, and everybody was in bed and sound asleep. Anyway, we got to the Edmonton Hotel, which was the mission headquarters. When the train stopped, there were two elders waiting for us, one of whom was Elder Ellwood. They picked us up and took us over to the mission home. I hadn’t been there very long when the phone rang, and it was Jack McLaughlin from Holbrook, Arizona. I had no idea who he was, but he knew I was coming from Arizona, and Holbrook was where I was supposedly coming from. He called and talked to me, and I really appreciated that; it took away a little bit of the homesickness I felt, even though I didn’t know him.

text: Here’s a clear framework for comparing the histories of Western and Eastern civilizations through the lens of storytelling—both oral and written. This approach emphasizes narrative as a medium of cultural memory, identity, and value transmission.

title: Better Stories
section: Framework for Comparison: Western vs. Eastern Civilizations Through Storytelling
text:
Framework for Comparison: Western vs. Eastern Civilizations Through Storytelling

1. Introduction

Purpose: Explain that civilizations are not only shaped by events, but by the stories they tell about themselves.
Scope: Focus on oral traditions, epic poetry, religious texts, philosophical treatises, and early written histories.
Thesis: Storytelling reveals not just historical facts, but cultural values, worldviews, and methods of preserving collective memory.




2. Foundations of Storytelling
Western Civilization:

Oral epics like The Iliad and The Odyssey (Greek) set patterns for heroism, individual agency, and human struggle.
Roman histories (Livy, Tacitus) combine narrative with moral lessons and civic ideals.
Early Christian texts reinterpret history through spiritual and moral frameworks.

Eastern Civilization:

Epic narratives such as Mahabharata and Ramayana (India) integrate philosophy, dharma, and cosmic order into human stories.
Chinese historiography (Sima Qian’s Records of the Grand Historian) emphasizes moral example, ancestor veneration, and dynastic cycles.
Oral storytelling (folk tales, parables, myths) preserves social norms, cosmology, and spiritual teachings.

Comparison Lens:

Western stories often focus on individual heroism, linear time, and civic duty.
Eastern stories often focus on cosmic order, ethical duty (dharma/dao), and cyclical time.




3. Oral Traditions

Medium: Poetry, songs, folklore, ritual performances.
Western: Bards, traveling storytellers, and minstrels convey heroic deeds, civic virtues, and historical memory.
Eastern: Storytelling as didactic tool, often intertwined with ritual, music, and performance; preserves philosophical and religious principles.

Analysis:

How oral storytelling shapes memory, identity, and moral values.
Transmission: communal vs. individual focus; heroic vs. moralistic narratives.




4. Written Histories

Western:

Greek and Roman histories as secular narratives emphasizing cause and effect, human agency, and moral judgment.
Chronological records in medieval Europe (e.g., chronicles, annals) frame events within divine providence.

Eastern:

Chinese dynastic histories: meticulous records emphasizing moral lessons and governance.
Indian and Southeast Asian texts: mytho-historical blending, ethical guidance, and cosmological context.


Analysis:

The role of literacy in preserving and codifying narratives.
Tension between factual recording and moral/philosophical interpretation.




5. Themes and Values in Stories

Western: Heroism, conflict, democracy, justice, moral choice, progress.
Eastern: Harmony, duty, moral virtue, cyclical time, cosmic order, spiritual enlightenment.
Compare how each civilization’s stories reflect social structure, governance, ethics, and worldview.




6. Evolution and Adaptation

Western: Shift from oral to manuscript to print culture; narratives adapted for nation-building, religion, and philosophy.
Eastern: Oral and written traditions often coexist; storytelling adapted for dynastic, religious, and philosophical continuity.

Discussion:

Influence of storytelling on literature, politics, and cultural identity.
How myths and histories evolve with society but preserve core values.




7. Conclusion

Summarize the key differences and commonalities in how civilizations record, transmit, and interpret history through stories.
Reflect on the significance of storytelling as a lens to understand human thought, social cohesion, and cultural memory.
Suggest relevance for today: global perspectives, cross-cultural understanding, and comparative historiography.

title: Classification
text:
Usually as end result of curiosity and at times necessity, we label or classify things in life.
Makes it easier to identify, categorize and find proper place.
Likewise, it may be convenient to classify people based on the outward appearance
Or all the things that should not be a reason for comparison.
race, color, religion, sex, national origin, age (40+), disability, or genetic information.

My mother can be categorized as an immigrant from Korea.

And if her father lived past 30 years of age, things would have turned out differently.

As a land and business owner and an eldest daughter of thriving businessmen, she would be educated and married to a prominent family in the region.

title: Letters Home
text:
During a dozen year period, we received 16 independent accounts from multiple locations.
The correspondence began as physical letters and electronic mails.
Slowly transitioning to all eMails.
These weekly communications were engaging, enlightening, as well as entertaining.
Some letters were like snapshots or a postcard, whereas some were written like a short story.
In fact, we received some printed photographs that gave way to a digital image file transmitted electronically.
We were living vicariously.
Visiting places through minds, eyes and hearts of dedicated, young individuals.

My siblings and I received letters and emails from 8 missionaries.
Through Sister K, received 8 additional eyewitness accounts.
From islands of sea: Micronesia, Kyushu/Okinawa, Taiwan, Hong Kong, Madagascar, and Scotland/Ireland to mainlands of North America; Massachusetts, Long Island, Washington, and California and Asia; Korea.
Eagerly waiting for that appointed time when they would send us their weekly events, happenings and experiences.
Heard highlights but sometimes understanding things they could not share.
Thoughtful way of minimizing our worries.
Seeing and feeling their growth.


To observers, the 18 or 24 months seem to be a relatively short duration.
Not to the families of those missionaries.
Recipients of the words and images from the field.
Experiencing, savouring and growing with each missionary.

Welcomed home these heroes at the old Salt Lake City Airport.
Multiple families would gather at the bottom of the escalator.
Inquiry began with the pilots and flight attendants

Which flight is this?

Then the balance of the passengers would pass by.
Triumphantly a group of missionaries appear.
Some maintain their composure, others ran.
Reserving their biggest hugs for their mothers.
While fathers are relegated to taking photographic or videographic images.
Siblings are biggest supporters.
Meanwhile grandparents are in the background and remember their younger days.

My mother kept a number of journals.
Writing about her experiences and sharing some of her recipes.

title: Mahler’s 2nd Symphony
text:
AI Summary
Gustav Mahler’s Symphony No. 2 in C minor (“Resurrection”) (premiered 1895) is over a century old, yet it continues to resonate with audiences and performers worldwide. Its relevance today comes from a mix of musical innovation, emotional depth, and timeless themes.

title: Mahler’s 2nd Symphony
text:
Why Mahler’s 2nd Still Matters Today

1. Universal Themes

The symphony wrestles with life, death, despair, hope, and transcendence.
Mahler takes the listener from funeral rites (first movement) through struggles, irony, and grief, to an overwhelming vision of renewal and resurrection.
These are existential questions that remain as urgent in the 21st century as they were in Mahler’s time.



2. Scale and Power

One of the first truly monumental symphonies: massive orchestra, organ, vocal soloists, and chorus.
Modern audiences still find the sheer sonic impact overwhelming — it fills concert halls in ways few works can.
The finale’s choral eruption of “Aufersteh’n, ja aufersteh’n wirst du” (“You will rise again”) is often described as a life-changing moment in live performance.



3. Bridge Between Eras

Combines Romantic tradition (Beethoven, Brahms) with innovations pointing toward 20th-century modernism.
Its use of folk-like melodies, irony, collage of styles, and spiritual searching prefigures Shostakovich, Stravinsky, and even film music.



4. Resonance with Crisis and Renewal

After wars, pandemics, and social upheavals, audiences connect with its narrative of struggle → collapse → renewal.
It’s often programmed in times of mourning or remembrance (e.g., after 9/11, orchestras turned to it for healing).



5. Personal Connection

Mahler wrote the work while grappling with mortality and meaning. His deeply personal struggle gives the symphony an authentic voice that transcends its era.
Today, listeners facing their own uncertainties hear their emotions mirrored in the music.

title: Mahler’s 2nd Symphony
text:
In short
Mahler’s Resurrection Symphony endures because it is more than music — it’s an experience of grief, hope, and transcendence. Its emotional honesty, monumental sound, and universal questions keep it fresh, urgent, and profoundly moving for modern audiences.

성남, 서산, 강남, 군산, 청주, 천안.

18 months and 24 months away from the comforts of a home is a sacrifice.
In some sense, this is an adventure, a spiritual one.
Many are visiting and sampling countries and cultures around the globe.

How much time is necessary time to be immersed in a culture and understand its influence on people?

A consistent exposure to culture and an increased understanding of the language helps.
Always taken back by the language comprehension and command of nuance and subtlety of 사투리 (dialect) by those returning from the Korean Language Missions.

When is your nephew coming home? He just came home last Thursday.

Great question — Lincoln’s trip to Gettysburg for the dedication of the Soldiers’ National Cemetery in November 1863 is very well documented.
Departure: President Lincoln left Washington, D.C. on November 18, 1863, at about noon.
Mode of travel: He traveled by special train from the Baltimore & Ohio Railroad depot (near today’s Capitol Hill).
Route: Washington → Baltimore → Hanover Junction, Pennsylvania → Gettysburg. At Hanover Junction, the train transferred to the Hanover Branch Railroad to reach Gettysburg.
Arrival: Lincoln arrived in Gettysburg early evening on November 18 (around 6 p.m.).
👉 That means the trip took roughly 6 hours from departure in Washington to arrival in Gettysburg.
The next morning, November 19, 1863, he delivered the Gettysburg Address at the cemetery dedication.


Lincoln’s Travel Route to Gettysburg – November 18, 1863
1. Boarded in Washington, D.C., traveled south to Baltimore

President Lincoln departed from Washington, D.C., and took a Baltimore & Ohio (B&O) Railroad train south to Baltimore’s Camden Station.(HISTORY, Wikipedia)
2. Transferred in Baltimore and continued via Northern Central Railway

From Camden Station, Lincoln and his entourage continued north via the Northern Central Railway, heading toward Pennsylvania.(Wikipedia, American Civil War Forums)
3. Change of trains at Hanover Junction

At Hanover Junction, Lincoln transferred from the Northern Central Railway to the Hanover Branch Railroad, which would convey him directly west to Gettysburg.(Wikipedia, Gettysburg Daily, ExplorePAHistory)
4. Arrival at the Gettysburg Lincoln Railroad Station

He arrived at the Gettysburg Railroad Station (also known as the Lincoln Railroad Station) by dusk. From there, he was escorted to the Wills House to prepare his address.(gettysburgfoundation.org, Abraham Lincoln Online)



Route Summary (Visual & Narrative)


Washington, D.C. → Baltimore (B&O Railroad)

Baltimore → Hanover Junction (Northern Central Railway)

Hanover Junction → Gettysburg (Hanover Branch Railroad)

Arrival in Gettysburg — greeted and escorted to his lodging at the Wills House


This rail journey was significant not only for its logistical coordination—switching between lines at Hanover Junction—but also for enabling Lincoln to arrive in time to finalize his speech and participate in the dedication of the National Cemetery the following morning.

Appendix B: AI Explanation of 한옥
한옥(韓屋)은 한국의 전통적인 건축 양식으로 지어진 집을 의미합니다. 주로 나무, 흙, 돌, 짚 등을 사용하여 지어지며, 온돌, 대청마루 등 특징적인 구조를 가지고 있습니다. 넓은 의미로는 초가집, 너와집 등 모든 전통 가옥을 포함하지만, 일반적으로는 기와집 형태의 한옥을 떠올리는 경우가 많습니다. [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]
한옥의 특징:
• 온돌: 구들을 이용해 바닥 난방을 하는 한국 고유의 난방 방식입니다. [7, 7, 8, 8]
• 대청마루: 거실과 같이 넓은 공간으로, 여름철 시원하게 지낼 수 있는 공간입니다. [7, 7, 9, 9, 10, 11, 12]
• 처마: 지붕의 끝 부분이 건물 밖으로 길게 뻗어 나와 여름철 햇볕을 가려주고 겨울철에는 눈과 비를 막아줍니다. [7, 7, 13, 13]
• 자연과의 조화: 풍수지리 사상에 따라 자연 환경과 조화를 이루도록 지어지며, 뒤로는 산을 등지고 앞으로는 물을 바라보는 방향으로 짓는 것이 일반적입니다. [1, 1, 14, 14]
한옥의 종류:
• 초가집: 짚으로 지붕을 이은 집입니다. • 너와집: 나무 판자를 엮어 지붕을 이은 집입니다. • 기와집: 기와로 지붕을 이은 집입니다. [5, 5, 7, 7]
한옥의 장점:

text:
손자(孫子):
Hi Grandpa, came across some digital photos from the year of the Snake (乙巳)1.
Wasn’t this the period when you were slowing down and transitioning from company funded trips?
The photos told a different story.
Older Me:
That was the year the oldest of your maternal uncles got married, Uncle JH.
Yes, that was post company sponsored travel days. And I thought of taking things slower but your grandma had other ideas.
She was invited to the wedding in Korea and scheduled to travel there.
But I wasn’t – initially.
Like many things in life, women’s willpower changes the outcome.
Soon, I was making travel plans and thinking of people and places to meet and visit.
손자(孫子):
So how did you go about detailed planning? Without specifics of business trips.
Older Me:
We have visited Korea a number of times, but this was the first time only 2 of us traveled.
At that time we had sold the business that required the attention of grandma. Because I was working at the time, chose a 10-day visit duration. Planned around the wedding.
That opened up many options and possibilities.
In addition, a direct flight to Incheon, Korea, had begun just few weeks prior to the visit.2
I had a number of aunts and uncle that were in their 80s and 90s.
My mother’s younger siblings in Korea were, 90 and 87.
My father’s youngest brother was 82.
My mother’s church friend was 90.
Visiting them was my priority.
Plus I wanted to visit my hometown 인천(仁川).
The remaining time would be spent either shopping or visiting sites around the country.
I didn’t know how we could do all of this in 10 days.
We decided to visit 서울성전 at the beginning and at the end of our visit.
And met with the uncle and aunts, the first 4 days we were in Korea.
손자(孫子):
I do remember stories about your aunts and uncles.
I am glad you kept in touch with them over the years.
How did you get in touch with Grandma’s friends, after she had passed away?
Older Me:
We formed a group, LLJK, (이이정강).
We first met in 인천, during the early days of the Church in the area.
We had maintained our friendship with the help of the group chat.
All but L1 had moved to the States, when I told L2 and J that I would be traveling to Korea, they suggested I get in touch with L1, who lived in 마포 area of 서울
L2 warned me that there aren’t many people that would remember me and advised me to visit and enjoy the local food.
L1 met me on a day that was 90+ degrees Farenheit and same amount of humidity.
I wanted to meet my aunt first and then tour the town.
I wondered why he kept avoiding a lunchtime rendenvous
As a compromise, we met at 9AM at 동인천역(東仁川駅)
By 10AM the weather was brutal, I was struggling with the heat and the hilly streets
As we walked, L1 rehearsed the history and people associated with the church in Incheon (인천)
Started in 중앙동, in a rented, converted 2-story building. Recall, one of the floor had a tatami (畳) floor.
Then a government property3 in 답동 was purchased and the existing building was renovated for church use.
Subsequently a new building was built on site. Eventually, all of the 인천 area wards were combined into a single meeting house in 주안.
손자(孫子):
Quite a day. You were lucky that L2 was available and willing to take you to places. How did it feel to walk around the places of birth and growth?
Older Me:
Things had changed dramatically in last 50 years. Except for few places that hadn’t changed, it was like many other places in modern Korea. Vertical growth and no green areas. Almost a feeling of visiting a foreign country.
Except, the memories of people and experiences. Meetings and activities in the old chapel.
Friends that still remember who I was and accept me as who I have become.
손자(孫子):
So did you visit your old church on Sunday?
Older Me:
Yes, I visited 인천1와드. That Ward was composed of the former, 답동, 송도, 주안 Wards
As we were driving towards the new building, I related the conversion story of my mother.
She had studied with the missionaries for nearly 2 years. But she still had some questions. She wrote them down.
When Harold B. Lee visited Korea and my mother attended the fireside All of mother’s questions were answered by the visiting general authority. Mom’s mind was set to join the church - intellectually
Then one afternoon, she dreamed a dream.
In the dream, there were 2 books. She could tell they were the Bible and the Book of Mormon. And a hand appeared and pointing to 2 books and touching them one by one said
She was ready to be baptized.
손자(孫子):
Thanks for sharing that. So did anyone recognize you?
Older Me:
L2 was correct, in a congregation of nearly 150 people only 3 people knew me. L2’s mother. L1’s sister and her husband.
I wondered if this will be similar to how we will be welcomed into the next life. There will be we may know and recognize but only a few would personally escort us through.
That person this time was L2’s mom.
She recounted how she and my mother served in the Stake Primary Presidency, without really understandint the calling.
Then she recounted my mother’s dream about the hand and 2 books. Almost word for word.
My testimony was strengthened. I had come home to my and my family’s Bountiful.
Thank you members of the 인천 area. In particular, thank you Sister 임윤님, Brother 유관종, Sister 이강주. For remembering me, welcoming me, and confirming the faith of my parents.

Recent visit to a large, modern, metropolitan area confirmed a theory.
A suspicion that has been building and partially tested over the years.
I have become a country mouse than a city mouse.
All of the modern conveniences were present.
Clean, well organized streets with buses and subways that served virtually all parts of the city.
Law abiding citizens, adding to the sense of well being and safety.
Modern office and apartment buildings that housed hundreds if not thousand persons in a single edifice.
Places that will satisfy basics as well as un-stated needs in an instant.
In fact, the only thing missing were more customers that will consume all of the material goods that were readily available in this metropolitan area and beyond.
There were few things that I needed coaching up to become more like the citizen of this city.
Like navigating the maze of the underground transportation system. Calling taxis using the new peer to peer network. Ordering food through installed kiosks at each table.
In time, I would become more proficient and could mimic being a local person.
However, there was one trend that proved to be difficult to overlook.
Tasks in big city were mostly transactional.
No room, or more accurately no time for getting personal or have a human interaction.
In an area, covered with as if 人山人海, I felt alone. Tides of people in the morning and even more people in the evening hours.
I would not know how to adjust to this setting where people appear to congregate and get things done, then retire to their areas of refuge, into their cubicles in the sky.
I could adjust, but given a choice, I will take a small town with its inconveniences over a big town living.

title: Notes
text:
1. Steps to Donate Assets


Form the Foundation


Incorporate as a nonprofit corporation in your state (usually via Secretary of State).

Adopt bylaws and appoint a board of directors.

Apply for IRS recognition of tax-exempt status (Form 1023).



Transfer Ownership of Assets


Automobiles: Title must be transferred to the foundation’s name at the DMV.

Office equipment (computers, furniture, printers): Use a Bill of Sale or Donation Agreement transferring ownership to the foundation.

Keep detailed records (serial numbers, VINs, condition reports).



Value the Assets


Cars: Use IRS fair market value guides (Kelley Blue Book, Edmunds) to determine donation value.

Equipment: Appraisal or fair market estimate (Craigslist/eBay comps, or a professional appraisal if large).

Required: IRS Form 8283 (Noncash Charitable Contributions) if the donation is over $500; appraisal required if over $5,000.



Record the Contribution


Foundation records the donation as an in-kind contribution at fair market value.

Donor receives a donation receipt issued by the foundation.



IRS Filing


Donor claims the deduction on Schedule A (Form 1040).

Foundation records the contribution on its annual Form 990-PF.

title: Notes
text:
2. Benefits for the Donor
✅ Immediate Charitable Deduction


Donor can deduct the fair market value of the assets (subject to IRS limits — usually up to 30% of AGI for private foundation gifts).


✅ Avoid Capital Gains Tax


If the asset has appreciated (e.g., office equipment purchased cheaply but still valuable), donor avoids capital gains by donating instead of selling.


✅ Control Over Philanthropy


Unlike giving directly to a public charity, donating to your own foundation allows you (and family/board) to decide how funds and assets are used.


✅ Legacy Building


The foundation becomes a permanent vehicle for charitable giving in your family’s or business’s name.

title: Notes
text:
3. Benefits for the Foundation
✅ Seed Assets


Automobiles can be used for foundation operations (transporting materials, outreach) or sold to raise cash.

Office equipment reduces startup costs for administration.


✅ Tax-Free Growth


Once assets are sold, the foundation can reinvest proceeds tax-free (except small excise taxes).


✅ Operational Independence


The foundation starts with physical assets and potentially liquid cash from asset sales, giving it capacity to begin grantmaking.

title: Notes
text:
4. Example: Donating Automobiles & Equipment


You transfer a $15,000 car and $10,000 worth of office equipment to your new private foundation.

You receive a $25,000 charitable deduction on your personal taxes (subject to 30% AGI limit).

The foundation can use the car for operations and the office equipment for administration — or sell them to create a $25,000 starting fund for grants.



⚠️ Important Notes


The foundation must use or liquidate the assets for charitable purposes only.

Donor (or family) can’t use the car/equipment for personal benefit after donation (that’s self-dealing, strictly prohibited).

Large noncash donations (> $5,000) usually require a qualified appraisal to substantiate deduction.

Public Charity vs. Private Foundation
Great question! Here’s a clear breakdown of the difference between a Public Charity and a Private Foundation under IRS §501(c)(3):

title: Notes
text:
1. Common Ground
Both Public Charities and Private Foundations are nonprofit organizations recognized by the IRS under 501(c)(3). That means they are:


Tax-exempt on income related to their charitable purpose.

Eligible to receive tax-deductible donations.

Organized for purposes like religion, education, scientific research, arts, or relief of the poor.

title: Notes
text:
2. Public Charity
Definition:


A public charity is a 501(c)(3) that receives broad public support (from many donors, government grants, or program revenue).


Key Features:


Funding source: Must get a significant portion of income (at least 1/3 in many cases) from the general public, other charities, or government.

Examples: Churches, schools, hospitals, universities, museums, food banks.

Control: Usually governed by a diverse board, not a small group or family.

IRS Oversight: Generally lighter than private foundations.

Donor Tax Deduction: Donors can deduct up to 60% of AGI (adjusted gross income) for cash gifts.

title: Notes
text:
3. Private Foundation
Definition:


A private foundation is a 501(c)(3) that usually has a single major funding source (like a family, individual, or corporation).


Key Features:


Funding source: Funded primarily by one person, family, or company, not broad public support.

Examples: Gates Foundation, Ford Foundation, family foundations.

Control: Often run by its founders, family members, or a small group.

IRS Oversight: Heavier reporting and operating restrictions.

Payout Requirement: Must distribute at least 5% of assets annually for charitable purposes.

Excise Tax: Pays a small excise tax on investment income.

Donor Tax Deduction: Donors can deduct up to 30% of AGI for cash gifts.

Would you like me to also explain how the IRS decides whether a new nonprofit is classified as a public charity or private foundation by default (hint: new 501(c)(3)s are usually private foundations unless they qualify for public charity status)?
Perfect — let’s go into how the IRS actually classifies a new 501(c)(3) organization at the start:

title: Notes
text:
Default Rule


When you apply for IRS 501(c)(3) recognition (Form 1023), the IRS by default classifies you as a Private Foundation.

Why? Because it’s easier to assume one person/family is funding you until you prove otherwise.

title: Notes
section: How to Qualify as a Public Charity
text:
How to Qualify as a Public Charity
To be recognized as a Public Charity instead of a Private Foundation, you must meet one of the following tests:

1. Institutional Public Charities (Automatic Public Charity)
Some organizations are always considered public charities, regardless of funding:


Churches, synagogues, temples, mosques

Schools, colleges, universities

Hospitals and medical research organizations

Governmental units (when acting for charitable purposes)





2. Public Support Test
For most other nonprofits, the IRS checks whether you have broad public support:


One-Third Support Test:

At least 33⅓% of your total support must come from the public (individuals, government grants, other charities).

Facts and Circumstances Test (10% Test):

If you get at least 10% public support and can show you are actively seeking broad support (fundraising, grants, memberships), you may still qualify as a public charity.





3. Supporting Organizations
Some nonprofits qualify as supporting organizations if they are organized and operated exclusively to support one or more existing public charities (e.g., a “friends of the library” group).

title: Notes
section: What Happens if You Don’t Qualify?
text:
What Happens if You Don’t Qualify?


If you can’t show enough public support → the IRS will classify you as a Private Foundation.

But: You can later convert to public charity status if your donor base broadens.

title: Notes
text:
Key Takeaway


All new 501(c)(3)s start as private foundations by default.

To be a public charity, you must either:


Be in an automatically qualified category (church, school, hospital, etc.), OR

Pass the public support test (show enough donors/grants).

title: A 2 Minute Drama
text:
Key Characteristics of 한국가곡:
Lyrics in Korean
Unlike Western lieder (like Schubert or Schumann), Korean art songs are sung in standard Korean, often using poetry by modern Korean poets or texts that evoke traditional Korean values and imagery.
Western Musical Form
The structure, harmony, and vocal techniques are borrowed from Western classical music, particularly the German lied and French mélodie traditions.
Emphasis on Emotion (정서, jeong-seo)
Themes often revolve around longing, nature, love, nostalgia, and han (한) — the uniquely Korean feeling of deep sorrow or unresolved grief.
Piano Accompaniment
Most Korean art songs are composed for a solo voice with piano, similar to Western art songs.
Performance Tradition

These songs are frequently performed in recitals, competitions, and school curriculums for vocal students in Korea.

title: Convenience and Comfort
text:
Visited a place where food was fit for Goldilocks.
It wasn’t too spicy, too salty, but just right.
Took many photos, some came out better than I expected.
In fact, all of them were technically just right, as algorithm dictated it to be.
Didn’t have to make any travel plans.
Hosts took care of it, I just had to be ready and they chauffeured me from places to places using the latest navigation tools.

During the visit, I didn’t get lost – while we were with locals.
Consequently, I never learned how to figure out directions or where I was visiting.
By looking at metadata on photos, I could retrace places I visited.
In the days past, I would be asking directions even after planning with physical maps.
Looking for landmarks, such as banks or natural indicators that provides directional anchors.
Also studying the sun’s position aided in determining the direction in the absence of landmarks such as mountains.
This approach was mistake-prone but after a day or so, one usually figured out the lay of the land.






Figure 1: 창덕궁, near 37°34’45.4”N 126°59’32.4”E




One rainy afternoon, I ventured out on my own.
Initial thinking was that I could locate palaces, since most landmarks remained same in that part of town.
I miscalculated.
My assistant was the locally made, on-line map, which had details often lacking multi-purpose maps made outside the country.
However, since I couldn’t figure out my current location, the e-Maps were not as helpful.
To figure out the immediate location, I had to move about, which was difficult to notice on a small phone screen.
Finally resorted to asking people where I needed to go.
Some were friendly and some were helpful, some were neither.
At last, tried the strategy of following tourists to the tourist destination.






Figure 2: Within 비원



Food was not only presented well and flavored ideally, but also there were over abundance of it.
Growing up, food was scarce and meals were served plain.
We mostly ate vegetables, fishes and occasional meat-enhanced soups.
Food was local and seldom got to taste cuisine from other locations
We tasted meat, a couple times a year, usually during holidays or birthdays of older people.
On this trip, we got to sample food from all regions of the country, while in the capital city.
Special occasion food was available on-demand, all hours of the day.
One could eat food from days gone by as well as order food that was from other countries.
At a wedding banquet, the buffet line featured 5 separate offerings.
A line of traditional Korean food, followed by seafood selection, fruit and salad, and dessert.
An hour and half allotted time was not enough to sample all the food and to visit with relatives.^[in the wedding venues, scheduled are tightly set and each couple has 30 to 40 minutes to use the main hall and guests are directed to the dining hall afterwards, before the next couple starts their cycle of activities]
Chose to visit with relatives, for some it was nearly 30 years since we last saw them.






Figure 3: Closer to Food from earlier years



The society had transformed from scarcity and inconvenient mode to one of utmost abundance and comfort.
During 50 years, the pace of growth and transformation has been remarkable.
Kudos to the people of Korea their achievements that borders on miracle.
As an observer of the change, it seemed that in days of past, one was faced with daily challenges and inconvenience.
Lack of food and walk to nearly all places.
In the present day, there are more food than the population 2 or 3 times can consume.
In addition, one has to look for ways to exercise, to find a way to walk to places and and try to get lost and try the personal navigation skills rather than rely on electronic help.

Not to suggest that those days were preferable to present day.
Days of poverty, hunger and physical demands
But in some ways, discomfort, pain and hardship allowed for and provided comparison and appreciation.
And perhaps a slow build up of character.
Is there a way to accomplish it, during these Goldilocks days?

title: Reed J Irvine
text:
IRVINE, Reed (John) 1922-2004
OBITUARY NOTICE— See index for CA sketch: Born September 29, 1922, in Salt Lake City, UT; died of complications following a stroke November 16, 2004, in Rockville, MD. Consumer advocate, economist, and author. Irvine was the founder of the watchdog group Accuracy in Media (AIM). A graduate of the University of Utah, where he earned a B.A. in 1942, Irvine acted as an intelligence officer in the Pacific theater during World War II. After the war, he returned to school, first at the University of Washington and then attending Oxford University on a Fulbright scholarship. He graduated from Oxford in 1951 and was hired as an economist at the Federal Reserve System board of governors. From 1963 until 1977 he was international finance adviser for the Far East section. It was while working for the Federal Reserve that he got his idea to form AIM out of frustration with what he considered to be the slanted liberal perspective of the media. Founded in 1969, AIM often worked to get equal air time on television and space in newspapers for its more conservative views, and Irvine also wrote a syndicated column that was printed in about one hundred newspapers. The organization saw its most influential period during the years Ronald Reagan was president, declining somewhat in the 1990s as Irvine became increasingly preoccupied with investigating conspiracy theories, such as his belief that the crash of TWA Flight 800 was caused by a missile and that White House deputy counsel Vincent W. Foster Jr. might have actually been murdered, not a victim of suicide, in 1993. In 1985, Irvine started a venture similar to AIM, known as Accuracy in Academia, but its conservative agenda and desire to wield influence over academic freedoms found fewer sympathizers. Irvine remained chair of AIM until 2003, when he retired as chairman emeritus. He was the author of Media Mischief and Misdeeds (1984).

from Encyclopedia.com, https://www.encyclopedia.com/arts/educational-magazines/irvine-reed-john-1922-2004


Accuracy in Academia (AIA)’s founder, Reed Irvine, died November 16, 2004 at the age of 82. Born in 1922, he served his country in World War II as a marine. He really never stopped serving his country.
He started Accuracy in Media (AIM), AIA’s parent organization, in 1969, to scrutinize the then-dominant old media at a time when few questioned its reporting. From the time he retired as a Federal Reserve Board economist in the 1970s until late last year, when he suffered a serious heart attack, he worked for AIM full-time.
It is fair to say that the so-called new media—Fox News, talk radio and even internet blogs—that prove the reporting of the venerable CBS News and company to be inaccurate are rushing through a door that Reed Irvine opened when he started going head-to-head with media heavyweights such as then-Washington Post editor Ben Bradlee.
Reed Irvine started AIA in 1985 because he saw that too many professors were using classrooms the way that too many reporters used newsrooms—to influence events rather than provide actual accounts of the past and present. He served as chairman of AIA until his death.
Since the 1980s, his standards have guided AIA. In his late seventies, he went toe to toe with demonstrators who attempted to disrupt an AIA conference at Columbia University in New York City.
When I first came to AIA last year, I read an e-mail that Reed forwarded around the office. He answered one of AIM’s critics by writing, “Show me one thing that we have written that is inaccurate.” No one could.
On October 22, 1985, Izvestiya, the state-run newspaper in the then-still existent Soviet Union, ran an article on the founding of Accuracy in Academia (AIA). Of all of the press coverage that AIA has received in its history, the Izvestiya write-up is arguably the most historically significant. Entitled ‘The Hunt For Freethinkers,’ the piece took aim at the then-infant group’s purpose.
“By the look of things, henceforth students, with the start of their activities, will take out fountain pens and tape recorders,” Izvestiya predicted. “Teachers at universities are quivering with fear,” the Soviet press organ reported. “They tremble at the utterance of each word.”
“For who knows?,” Izvestiya asked rhetorically. “Are the students taking notes on their lectures for their own purposes, or are they listening for the purpose of reporting what the teacher says to the ultra-right organization, Accuracy in Academia?”
Izvestiya normally confined itself to attacking U. S. government policies and American society in general. Leveling a front-page broadside at a small non-profit group represented somewhat of an editorial departure for the journal. The attention Izvestiya devoted to AIA, then, gave the watchdog group quite a distinction.
“The reactionary newspaper, The Washington Times, crows over the report that Accuracy in Academia, which has only existed for a few days, already has gathered voluntary informants on 110 university campuses throughout the United States,” Izvestiya noted.
“At the call of their spiritual mentor, worshippers and apprentices of McCarthy hunt for teachers who have the courage to adhere to liberal convictions,” according to Izvestiya. The McCarthy that Izvestiya refers to is the late Sen. Joseph R. McCarthy, R-WI, famous for his investigations of communists in U. S. government jobs.
“By such measures, these teachers are labeled ‘Marxists,’ which in contemporary America is pregnant with the most serious consequences,” Izvestiya asserted. “For example, political science professor Bertell Ollman knows this from personal experience for he dared admit that he was actually on the side of Marxism. Solely because of that he was not allowed to compete to fill a position at the University of Maryland.”
Six years after the Izvestiya article appeared, the Soviet Union itself imploded and the Cold War ended. This year, AIA celebrates 19 years of life and is still in business. Izvestiya is still in business too, although under new management. And by the way, so is Bertell Ollman. A professor of politics at New York University, he teaches ‘Socialist Theory’ for undergraduates and ‘Communism’ and ‘Methods of Political and Social Analysis’ at the graduate level.
Because professors such as Ollman, and their understudies, are still in business, teaching the history of the Cold War from the Evil Empire’s perspective, AIA continues its work, as our founder would have wanted us to.
Accuracy in Academia founder, Reed Irvine,
died November 16, 2004 at the age of 82.
His legacy as a true advocate of democracy lives on.
Reed Irvine, R. I. P.

title: Absolute Self-Effacement
text:
Humility is just as much the opposite of self-abasement as it is of self-exaltation.
To be humble is not to make comparisons.
Secure in its reality, the self is neither better nor worse, bigger nor smaller, than anything else in the universe.
It is–is nothing, yet at the same time one with everything.
It is in this sense that humility is absolute self-effacement.

To be nothing in the self-effacement of humility, yet, for the sake of the task, to embody its whole weight and importance in your earing, as the one who has been called to undertake it.
To give to people, works, poetry, art, what the self can contribute, and to take, simply and freely, what belongs to it by reason of its identity.
Praise and blame, the winds of success and adversity, blow over such a life without leaving a trace or upsetting its balance.”

Good question 👍 — the Han dynasty (206 BCE – 220 CE) produced, preserved, and canonized many of the foundational Chinese works on warfare, governance, and statecraft. Some were written earlier (in the Warring States or Qin) but became standards and official references during the Han. Here’s a structured overview:

title: Historian’s Records
text:
⚔️ Warfare & Military Thought

Sunzi Bingfa (孫子兵法, Art of War) – by Sun Tzu (pre-Han, ~5th century BCE)

Became canonical under the Han; generals like Han Xin applied its strategies.
Focus: deception, flexibility, and psychological warfare.

Wu Zi (吳子) – by Wu Qi (Warring States general).

Emphasized discipline, logistics, and civil-military relations.

Wei Liaozi (尉繚子) – a Qin/Han text.

Practical guidance for rulers: military organization, law, agriculture, governance linked to war-making.

Tai Gong’s Six Secret Teachings (太公六韜, Liutao) – attributed to Jiang Ziya (Zhou strategist).

Focus on civil and military balance, leadership, and moral authority in warfare.


👉 These, along with other texts, were later collected into the Seven Military Classics (武經七書) (canonized in the Song dynasty), but the Han dynasty already circulated and studied them.

title: Historian’s Records
text:
🏛️ Governance, Law, and Statecraft

Book of Documents (尚書, Shangshu)

Ancient collection of speeches and edicts; used in the Han as a Confucian classic for legitimizing rule.

Records of the Grand Historian (史記, Shiji) – by Sima Qian (c. 94 BCE)

Not a manual, but a massive history covering rulers, generals, and statecraft — provided models (good and bad) for governance.

Book of Han (漢書, Hanshu) – by Ban Gu (1st century CE)

Official dynastic history; detailed accounts of institutions, law, economy, and military campaigns.

The Spring and Autumn Annals (春秋, Chunqiu) + Commentaries

Treated as a Confucian manual of rulership and morality.

Huang-Lao Texts (黃老學) – blending Daoism, Legalism, and pragmatism.

Popular especially in the early Han for governance emphasizing minimal interference + strong law.

Statutes and Ordinances of the Second Year (二年律令, Ernian lüling)

Excavated Han legal code, showing actual laws enforced in governance.

title: Historian’s Records
text:
📌 Takeaway

Military standards: The Han revered earlier classics (Sunzi, Wuzi, Wei Liaozi, Liutao) as guides, with generals like Han Xin embodying their application.
Governance standards: Confucian classics (Shangshu, Chunqiu), historical works (Shiji, Hanshu), and legal codes shaped how emperors and officials ruled.
Together, these became the intellectual backbone of Han statecraft — a mix of Confucian morality, Legalist structure, and strategic pragmatism.

Great question. Sima Qian’s Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji) is not just a chronology—it’s a literary and philosophical work that weaves together history, biography, morality, and political thought. Here are the major themes scholars usually highlight:


1. The Mandate of Heaven & Cyclical History


Dynasties rise and fall because of virtue (de) or the loss of it.

Heaven grants or withdraws legitimacy depending on rulers’ morality and ability.

Shiji illustrates this cycle through narratives of Xia, Shang, Zhou, Qin, and Han.





2. Human Agency vs. Fate


Tension between individual choices and forces beyond control.

Figures like Xiang Yu (the failed conqueror) show the tragedy of brilliance undone by circumstance.

Sima Qian suggests that fate sets limits, but human judgment and character still matter.





3. Morality, Virtue, and Exemplars


History as moral instruction: good rulers uphold ritual, benevolence, and justice; bad rulers indulge in cruelty and excess.

Biographies highlight models (Confucius, ministers of Zhou) and warnings (tyrannical Qin Shi Huang, corrupt officials).





4. The Role of Officials and Advisors


Emphasis on the importance of wise ministers and loyal remonstrators.

Many biographies of courtiers, generals, and strategists stress loyalty, courage, or betrayal.

A warning that rulers who ignore good advice invite ruin.





5. The Ordinary and the Marginalized


Sima Qian breaks ground by including merchants, assassins, wandering knights, astrologers, jesters, etc.

These stories show that history is not only about kings but also about those at society’s edges.





6. Heroism and Tragedy


Admiration for bold individuals who challenge fate, even if they fail.

The tragic arcs of figures like Jing Ke (the would-be assassin of the Qin king) or Qu Yuan (the poet-statesman) highlight human dignity amid defeat.





7. Memory and Legacy


Sima Qian stresses the importance of recording deeds for posterity, even when the person failed in life.

His own preface, written after his disgrace and castration, underscores the theme: history gives people lasting voice beyond shame or death.





8. Integration of Myth, History, and Philosophy


The Shiji blends legendary origins (Yellow Emperor, Yao, Shun) with verifiable historical records.

It is both a Confucian moral history and an effort to preserve cultural memory as a unified narrative.



✅ In sum:

The Shiji is about the rise and fall of power, the tension between virtue and ambition, and the human struggle against fate. It’s simultaneously a political manual, a collection of moral biographies, and a deeply personal meditation on history and memory.

The Records of the Grand Historian (史記 Shǐjì) is one of the most important works in Chinese history and literature. Here’s an overview in plain, interview-style language:



What It Is


Written by Sima Qian (司馬遷), a court historian during the Han Dynasty (around 91 BCE).

It is the first comprehensive history of China, covering more than 2,000 years—from the legendary Yellow Emperor (~2600 BCE) through the reign of Emperor Wu of Han.

Contains 130 chapters, blending history, biography, philosophy, and storytelling.





Structure
The work is divided into five sections:


Basic Annals (本紀 Běnjì) – Chronicles of emperors and ruling houses.

Chronological Tables (年表 Niánbiǎo) – Timelines to keep events across states and dynasties aligned.

Treatises (書 Shū) – Thematic essays on subjects like music, economics, law, astronomy, and rituals.

Hereditary Houses (世家 Shìjiā) – Histories of feudal lords and major noble families.

Biographies (列傳 Lièzhuàn) – Lives of notable figures—officials, generals, scholars, foreign peoples, even assassins and merchants.





Why It Matters


Foundation of Chinese Historiography: Established the model for later dynastic histories (正史 Zhèngshǐ).

Literary Value: Written with vivid, often dramatic storytelling; sometimes reads like a novel.

Balanced Perspective: Sima Qian included both emperors and commoners, victors and rebels—unusual for ancient histories.

Moral Voice: Shows his Confucian values but also independence; Sima Qian himself suffered disgrace and castration yet still completed it, turning personal tragedy into a monumental legacy.





Influence


Considered the “father of Chinese history.”

Influenced later historians such as Ban Gu (Book of Han), and even Chinese prose style in general.

Still read today in China and worldwide for insights into leadership, politics, culture, and human character.



👉 In short: The Records of the Grand Historian is a sweeping, 2,000-year account of China’s past, written with literary flair and historical rigor, setting the standard for all future Chinese history writing.

American stop-motion animated fantasy film
Kubo and the Two Strings is a stop-motion animated fantasy steeped in Japanese folklore and myth. The film follows Kubo, a boy who can animate origami with music from his shamisen (a three-stringed instrument). He lives quietly, caring for his ill mother, until supernatural forces—his mother’s sisters and his grandfather, the Moon King—hunt him down.
To survive, Kubo embarks on a quest to find three magical items that once belonged to his father, a fallen samurai. Along the way, he is guided by Monkey and Beetle, companions who embody loyalty, sacrifice, and forgotten family ties.
The journey is both external and deeply personal: Kubo confronts loss, memory, and the stories that shape identity. Ultimately, instead of defeating his grandfather through violence, Kubo redefines the conflict through compassion and storytelling—transforming vengeance into remembrance and forgiveness.

title: Elsewhere
text:
American animated fantasy comedy-drama film
Coco (2017, Pixar/Disney) is an animated film set in Mexico that explores themes of family, memory, and cultural tradition through the lens of the Día de los Muertos (Day of the Dead).
The story follows Miguel, a 12-year-old boy who dreams of becoming a musician despite his family’s long-standing ban on music. When he secretly borrows a guitar from a shrine to his idol, the late singer Ernesto de la Cruz, he is magically transported to the Land of the Dead.
There, Miguel meets his ancestors and discovers family secrets—most importantly that de la Cruz is not the hero he seemed, and that his true great-great-grandfather is Héctor, a forgotten musician struggling to be remembered.
The film emphasizes that remembering and honoring loved ones keeps them alive in spirit, while being forgotten is a “final death.” By the end, Miguel reconciles his passion for music with his family’s values, restoring harmony between generations.

Memory & Storytelling: Coco focuses on remembering loved ones to keep them alive in spirit, while Kubo portrays storytelling as a weapon against oblivion, a way to transform grief into meaning.
Mortality & Loss: Both tackle death openly, but in different tones. Coco is tender, celebratory, and hopeful. Kubo is darker and melancholic, blending the inevitability of loss with the possibility of emotional survival.




Cultural Lens

Coco draws from Mexican traditions like Día de los Muertos, presenting a vibrant, colorful afterlife where joy and remembrance sustain family bonds.
Kubo takes inspiration from Japanese folklore and Buddhist ideas, with themes of impermanence, ancestral spirits, and transformation.




Tone & Style

Coco is musical, lively, and emotionally warm—its message is broadly accessible and uplifting.
Kubo is poetic, visually striking, and more contemplative, often leaning toward the somber beauty of myth.

Together, these films show two cultural perspectives on the universal human experiences of loss, memory, and family. Coco comforts us with the idea that love transcends death when we remember, while Kubo challenges us to face mortality with courage, compassion, and the transformative power of storytelling.

Who said to men: “Come, follow me,
That ye, my friends, with God may be.”
I believe in Christ—my Lord, my God!
My feet he plants on gospel sod;
I’ll worship him with all my might;
He is the source of truth and light.
I believe in Christ; he ransoms me.
From Satan’s grasp he sets me free,
And I shall live with joy and love
In his eternal courts above.
I believe in Christ; he stands supreme!
From him I’ll gain my fondest dream;
And while I strive through grief and pain,
His voice is heard: “Ye shall obtain.”
I believe in Christ, so come what may,
With him I’ll stand in that great day
When on this earth he comes again
To rule among the sons of men.

Mahler’s 2nd Symphony: Resurrection in the 21st Century
Gustav Mahler’s Symphony No. 2, the “Resurrection,” stands as one of the most profound musical meditations on life, death, and the hope of transcendence. Composed in the late 19th century, it reflects Mahler’s own confrontation with mortality and spiritual longing. Yet more than a historical artifact, the symphony resonates powerfully in the 21st century, a world defined by rapid change, existential uncertainty, and the search for meaning.
Mahler’s era was one of societal tension and personal anxiety. The late Romantic period fostered grand artistic expression, yet Mahler’s life was marked by illness, loss, and the awareness of his own mortality. The Resurrection Symphony embodies this consciousness through its expansive five-movement structure. From the dramatic opening of the first movement, which confronts death directly, to the final choral adagio that envisions a spiritual awakening, the symphony charts a journey from despair to transcendence. Mahler’s orchestration—massive, intricate, and emotionally charged—invites listeners into an intimate yet universal experience, bridging personal grief and collective hope.
At the core of the symphony is a philosophical engagement with human existence. The first movement begins with somber motifs that evoke mortality, while the slow second movement offers introspection and lament. The vigorous scherzo of the third movement provides contrast, reflecting human resilience and vitality. Mahler then transforms the music in the fourth movement, introducing a contemplative, almost otherworldly quality through orchestral color and vocal text. The final movement, employing a full chorus and soloists, sets Friedrich Gottlieb Klopstock’s poetry to music, declaring the triumph of the spirit over death—a vision of resurrection that is both personal and communal.
Historically, the symphony challenged its early audiences with its scale and spiritual ambition, yet it influenced generations of composers, from Schoenberg to Shostakovich, and became a staple of concert repertoire. Today, its relevance extends beyond the concert hall. In the 21st century, Mahler’s exploration of mortality resonates amid global crises, pandemics, and climate change. The symphony’s trajectory—from despair to hope—mirrors the collective human need to confront uncertainty and find meaning, offering a form of emotional and spiritual catharsis.
Furthermore, Mahler’s integration of orchestral, choral, and textual elements anticipates contemporary multimedia approaches to art and performance. Modern productions often incorporate visual and technological enhancements, underscoring the symphony’s timeless capacity to engage audiences across disciplines. Its universal themes transcend culture and geography, uniting listeners in reflection, empathy, and communal experience—a reminder that music remains a powerful medium for shared human understanding.
In conclusion, Mahler’s Symphony No. 2 is far more than a monumental Romantic work; it is a living, breathing exploration of life’s ultimate questions. Its capacity to confront death, celebrate resilience, and imagine transcendence ensures its continued relevance. In an era marked by uncertainty, the Resurrection Symphony offers a musical framework for hope, collective reflection, and the enduring human spirit.

The act of controlling, limiting, or holding back one’s own actions, emotions, or impulses.

Example: “She showed restraint in responding to the provocative comment.”



Constraint:


A limitation or restriction imposed by an external factor or circumstance.

Often implies something enforced or obligatory, rather than chosen.

Example: “The project was completed under financial constraints.”

title: Something Much Bigger
text:
When I go photo hunting, Sister K expects updates:
Where I am.
How long until I’m done taking pictures.
When I’ll be home.
This time, I was at the 2,300-meter level, watching the fall colors shift on the eastern side of a mountain.
Maybe it’s because I’ve been to this spot before.
Or perhaps it’s because I now understand why leaves change color—
Not simply from temperature drops or elevation changes,
But from the shifting sunlight, the seasonal tilt of the Earth orbiting the sun.
Yet today, I couldn’t find a single tree or grove I hadn’t already captured a likeness or similar images before.
I messaged Sister K: I’m wrapping up, heading home.
One last turn-off.
I stayed in the car, pulled out both the DSLR and the phone camera, and captured an image.
Sister K replied with a link1:
Interviewer: What do you think happens when we die?
Interviewee: I don’t think we die. I don’t think we understand the divine concept of time… Something much bigger is going on than we’re aware of in our day-to-day routines. I don’t have the intelligence or the DNA makeup to answer that question.
There are many things I’ve come to understand. How certain mysteries of younger days have been explained as I work, learn and age.
And there are things I’m content not to know:
What comes after this existence.
It’s enough to know where I am,
And that I have a home to return to.
That I can speak in words and communicate through action.
That each have access to resources and places that explains a bit of eternity from our corner of existence.
